runs.text: This specification complements OPC 40100-1 and OPC 40100-2. It does not define machine-vision job orchestration, recipe or configuration management, or asset lifecycle management. OPC 40100-1 remains authoritative for jobs, system state, recipes, configurations and result transfer, and OPC 40100-2 remains authoritative for asset identity, component inventory, condition monitoring and maintenance. This specification extends those models with sensor acquisition semantics, media endpoints, calibration and coordinate frames, AI inference and provenance, defined result content, and feedback. Annex D defines the integration contract for a Server that exposes the same equipment through this specification and OPC 40100.

Two OPC UA machine vision companion specifications already exist, as well as a robotics one (OPC 40010-1). None of them describes the four things above. OPC 40100-1 orchestrates jobs but states that result content is
"application-specific and not defined at this time"

And no OPC UA specification describes an AI model. The evidence for each of these statements, with quotations and section numbers, is in
The consequence is that every vision integration is bespoke: two Servers can be fully conformant to the existing specifications and still be mutually unintelligible.

general.title: General information to vision and OPC UA

runs.text: A camera is one of the few devices on a plant floor whose output no OPC UA specification describes. A Server can publish a torque, a temperature and a machine state in an interoperable form, and then has no defined way to say what its vision system saw, which model interpreted it, or what the verdict actually means. Two Servers can be fully conformant to the existing machine vision specifications and remain mutually unintelligible.

The gap is not the imagery. Moving pixels is a solved problem, and this document deliberately does not try to solve it again — media is obtained by reference, from an endpoint the Server describes. What is missing is everything around the imagery: which sensor produced it, how it is calibrated and in which coordinate frame, what inference ran over it, what the result contains, and how a correction travels back.

This document defines those as one information model. A physical camera and a simulated sensor in a renderer expose the same members with the same meaning, so a client written against one works against the other, and synthetic data, training and the corrections coming off a production line all describe themselves in the same terms.

This document complements OPC 40100-1 and OPC 40100-2. It does not replace their machine-vision job orchestration, recipe and configuration management, result transfer, asset identity, condition monitoring or maintenance models.
